issue: No position instruction — user doesn't know whether to argue for or against
original_question: Should video games be allowed in school during lunch breaks?
suggested_rewrite: Should schools allow video games during lunch breaks? Pick a side and argue it.
new_tips: State your position in the first sentence
Give one concrete reason — focus on learning, well-being, or fairness
Acknowledge the strongest objection in one sentence before closing

issue: Directed at 'kids' — awkward for an adult user who has no stake in the premise; framing collapses for anyone past school age
original_question: Should kids be allowed to choose their own bedtimes?
suggested_rewrite: Should parents set strict bedtimes for young children, or let them self-regulate their sleep? Take a position.
new_tips: State your position clearly
Give one developmental or practical reason
Acknowledge what the opposing side gets right before closing

issue: Tips describe what to argue (individual freedom vs civic duty) rather than how to argue — they pre-script the content instead of coaching technique
original_question: Should voting be made mandatory for all citizens?
suggested_rewrite: Should voting be made mandatory for all citizens? Defend your position.
new_tips: State your position in the opening sentence
Give one clear reason — then concede the strongest objection before closing
End with a sentence that captures the core trade-off your position accepts

issue: 'Is breakfast the most important meal' has a factually contested answer (nutrition science doesn't support the claim) — makes both sides feel like arguing trivia rather than a real position
original_question: Is breakfast the most important meal of the day?
suggested_rewrite: Should people prioritize eating breakfast every day, or does skipping it have legitimate benefits? Take a side.
new_tips: Commit to one position
Give one reason rooted in health, performance, or practicality
Acknowledge that the answer may vary by person before landing your conclusion

issue: 'Is it better to own pets than not to?' is so personal and lifestyle-dependent that neither side is meaningfully defensible as a general claim — lacks a real debate axis
original_question: Is it better to own pets than not to?
suggested_rewrite: Should more people seriously consider getting a pet, or is the responsibility often underestimated? Argue your position.
new_tips: Take a clear stance on the general case, not just your personal preference
Give one benefit or one caution that applies broadly
Close with the key point your position hinges on

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_1-2_001 (school uniforms vs dress code) — both argue school clothing policy; covered twice in the same band
original_question: Should all schools have a dress code even if not full uniforms?
suggested_rewrite: Should schools regulate student clothing at all, or leave dress entirely to individual choice? Take a position.
new_tips: Distinguish your argument from the uniform debate — focus on the principle of any school clothing rule
Give one reason about identity, equity, or school environment
Close with the specific policy you'd support or oppose

issue: 'Is watching too much TV harmful?' presupposes 'too much' — yes by definition; makes arguing 'no' nearly impossible without redefining the premise
original_question: Is watching too much TV harmful?
suggested_rewrite: Is heavy television viewing harmful, or are the concerns overstated? Pick a side.
new_tips: Commit to yes or no on the general claim
Give one specific effect — cognitive, social, or physical — as your main evidence
Keep your argument focused and brief

issue: Exact near-duplicate of debate_3-4_007 — both ask 'Is a college degree still worth the cost?' in the same difficulty band
original_question: Is a college degree still worth the cost? Make your argument.
suggested_rewrite: Is a four-year university degree the best investment for most young people, or are alternatives like trade school and self-directed learning undervalued? Argue your position.
new_tips: State your position on the general case, not just for specific majors
Use one data point or example to support your argument
Acknowledge the strongest counterpoint in one sentence before concluding

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_1-2_002 (work from home vs office) promoted to band 3-4 with minimal added complexity — essentially the same question
original_question: Is remote work more productive than working in an office?
suggested_rewrite: Should companies default to remote work rather than in-office arrangements? Build the case for your position.
new_tips: Commit to a position on company policy, not personal preference
Support with two reasons: one about individual productivity, one about team or culture dynamics
Address the strongest objection before concluding

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_1-2_027 (specialist vs generalist career) — same question reframed with marginal added complexity in same mode
original_question: Is it better to specialize early in your career or stay generalist for longer?
suggested_rewrite: Does early specialization give you a stronger career foundation than staying generalist, or does depth come at the cost of adaptability? Make the case.
new_tips: Commit to one strategy and state it upfront
Give two supporting reasons: one about early outcomes, one about long-term trajectory
Address the risk of the path you chose

issue: 'Is it better for consumers to negotiate salary' — 'consumers' is a category error; salary negotiation involves employees, not consumers
original_question: Is it better for consumers to negotiate salary than accept the first offer?
suggested_rewrite: Should job candidates always negotiate their salary rather than accepting the first offer? Take a position.
new_tips: Commit to one strategy
Give one financial or relational reason
Acknowledge when accepting quickly might make sense before closing

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_3-4_025 — both debate proactive salary negotiation vs waiting; only a slight framing shift separates them
original_question: Is it better to negotiate a raise annually than wait to be recognized?
suggested_rewrite: Should employees proactively ask for raises on a regular schedule, or is it smarter to wait until the timing and leverage are right? Argue your position.
new_tips: Commit to one approach
Give one reason about outcomes — financial or relational
Address what your preferred approach risks before closing

issue: The framing 'when there are problems on Earth' stacks the question against space exploration — it's a rhetorical presupposition that the contrast is unfair, nudging users toward anti-space
original_question: Is space exploration a good use of public funding when there are problems on Earth? Argue your side.
suggested_rewrite: Should governments continue investing heavily in space exploration, or should that funding be redirected to solving more immediate problems? Argue your position.
new_tips: Acknowledge the tension directly — don't pretend the trade-off doesn't exist
Use one specific example of benefit or opportunity cost
Build toward a compelling conclusion that addresses what the other side gets right

issue: Third tip ('Address the specific failure mode of remote-first you acknowledge') is circular and confusing — it tells users to address a failure mode without first explaining what failure mode to pick
original_question: Is remote-first culture better for long-term company culture than hybrid models?
suggested_rewrite: Is remote-first culture better for long-term company culture than hybrid models? Take a position.
new_tips: Commit to a position on which model builds stronger culture over time
Give two reasons grounded in trust formation, collaboration, or equity
Concede the strongest counterpoint and explain why your position still holds

issue: The question asks whether AVs should be approved 'before human-level safety is proven' — this essentially pre-decides the answer (no, don't approve an unsafe technology); making the pro-approval side require arguing for an incoherent position
original_question: Should autonomous vehicles be approved for public roads before human-level safety is proven?
suggested_rewrite: Should autonomous vehicles be permitted on public roads now, even without conclusive proof they are safer than human drivers? Argue your position.
new_tips: Position yourself on the precautionary principle versus the cost of delay
Give two reasons: one about current safety data, one about the net harm from waiting
Address the liability and regulatory certification questions briefly

issue: Question asks if 'professional sports leagues' should pay college athletes — this conflates two separate institutions (NCAA vs pro leagues) and is factually confused; the debate is about the NCAA paying athletes, not the NFL or NBA paying them
original_question: Should professional sports leagues be required to pay college athletes?
suggested_rewrite: Should college athletes be compensated by their universities beyond scholarships? Argue your position.
new_tips: Position yourself on amateurism versus labor rights in college athletics
Give two reasons: one about revenue sharing, one about education mission or equity
Address the Title IX or competitive balance implications briefly

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_9-10_008 and debate_7-8_010 — all three ask about economic growth vs environmental/ecological sustainability; three prompts covering the same core tension across two adjacent bands
original_question: Is economic growth fundamentally incompatible with environmental sustainability? Make your case.
suggested_rewrite: Can economies achieve meaningful environmental sustainability without sacrificing growth, or is the green growth model fundamentally flawed? Make the case.
new_tips: Use specific data points on decoupling or resource throughput
Address green growth versus degrowth frameworks directly
Conclude with a synthesis that names the condition under which your position holds

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_7-8_003 and debate_9-10_008 — same economic growth vs. sustainability axis, third coverage of this theme across bands
original_question: Should nations prioritize GDP growth or ecological sustainability when they conflict?
suggested_rewrite: When economic growth and ecological sustainability conflict directly, which should governments prioritize, and why? Build a rigorous argument.
new_tips: State your position on the prioritization question — don't hedge by saying both matter
Give two reasons: one about long-run viability, one about distributional justice
Address who suffers most from each choice and why that matters to your argument

issue: 'Is hybrid work ultimately destroying organizational culture' — 'destroying' is loaded language that presupposes harm and makes the pro-hybrid side argue against a straw man framing
original_question: Is hybrid work ultimately destroying organizational culture compared to fully in-person?
suggested_rewrite: Does hybrid work weaken organizational culture compared to fully in-person work, or does it create a stronger, more equitable culture? Take a position.
new_tips: Define what a strong organizational culture means before arguing about which model achieves it
Give two reasons: one about trust formation, one about equity and access
Address the generational or role-specific variation in hybrid effectiveness

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_9-10_029 — both ask whether advanced AI systems should receive legal personhood / constitutional rights; differ only in the instruction to rebut 'top three counterpoints' vs address the corporate personhood analogy
original_question: Should we grant legal personhood to advanced AI systems? Construct a formal argument with rebuttals to the top three counterpoints.
suggested_rewrite: Should advanced AI systems be granted legal personhood? Build a formal argument that defines your threshold criteria and addresses the three most powerful objections.
new_tips: Build a philosophical framework for personhood — what criteria must be met and why
Anticipate and dismantle objections systematically: sentience, accountability, and corporate-personhood analogies
Close with the concrete legal or social implications if your position were adopted

issue: 'Should billionaires exist?' is ambiguous — it conflates should billionaires be taxed, should wealth accumulation be capped, and should the economic system be redesigned; users won't know which level of claim to argue
original_question: Should billionaires exist? Build a complete argument that addresses economic, moral, and systemic dimensions.
suggested_rewrite: Should societies place an effective cap on individual wealth, preventing anyone from accumulating billionaire-level fortunes? Build a complete argument addressing economic, moral, and systemic dimensions.
new_tips: Define your moral framework explicitly before making economic or systemic claims
Use data on wealth concentration to ground your argument
Address both incentive structures and systemic effects, and acknowledge the strongest counterargument

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_7-8_011 — both ask whether representative democracy is sufficient given modern complexity; the 9-10 version adds 'technical complexity' framing but covers the same core thesis
original_question: Is representative democracy as currently practiced sufficient to govern societies defined by deep technical complexity?
suggested_rewrite: Is representative democracy capable of producing technically competent governance in domains like AI, pandemics, and climate — or does its design structurally fail in high-complexity environments?
new_tips: Distinguish representation failures from epistemic failures — they require different remedies
Give two reasons: one about the knowledge gap between elected generalists and technical domains, one about temporal misalignment
Propose a specific institutional alternative or reform rather than leaving the critique abstract

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_7-8_035 — both ask whether the international financial architecture is biased against developing economies; the 9-10 version adds 'perpetuate underdevelopment' framing but covers the same mechanisms
original_question: Is the international financial system structurally biased against developing economies in ways that perpetuate underdevelopment?
suggested_rewrite: Is reform of the international financial system — IMF conditionality, dollar hegemony, sovereign debt structures — necessary to allow developing economies to escape structural disadvantage? Build your argument.
new_tips: Identify the specific mechanisms: original sin dynamics, reserve currency burden, or capital flow liberalization constraints
Give two reasons: one about policy space constraints, one about financial contagion or debt dynamics
Address the counterargument that integration has driven extraordinary growth in East Asia and why it doesn't undermine your position

issue: Near-duplicate of debate_9-10_001 — both argue whether AI systems should receive legal recognition / rights; differ only in framing ('capability thresholds' vs 'advanced AI systems')
original_question: Should AI systems that meet certain capability thresholds be subject to constitutional rights analogous to legal personhood?
suggested_rewrite: What legal obligations, if any, should societies have toward AI systems as they grow in capability? Argue for a specific framework — and defend it against the strongest objections.
new_tips: Define the capability threshold and the specific rights or obligations you're proposing before giving reasons
Give two reasons: one about moral status criteria, one about legal system design and accountability
Address the corporate personhood analogy, its functional rationale, and whether it applies to AI
